rv.q: LaTanya Richardson Jackson's star-studded Broadway revival of August Wilson's 'The Piano Lesson,' is, in a word, magnificent.
The play’s characters are so individually well-formed and collectively solid that their voices have a way of lingering in the mind, and Wilson's language is dramatic lyricism of a very high order.
This superb revival of August Wilson's 1987. Pulitzer Prize winner strikes all the right notes.
The script, which in 1990 earned the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, remains a thing of lyrical beauty.
All flowing here with eloquence and verve.
What the production — directed by LaTanya Richardson Jackson, wife of Samuel L. — never quite nails is the ghost story that hovers over the living room drama and how best to marry the two.
But when the melodies flow freely, the magnificent music rolls over you, just as the past continues to roll over characters struggling to move forward, its legacy forever a part of them.
That’s the nature of The Piano Lesson: It’s a play so much about the possibilities of the present that are cut off when other demands, like those of the past, make themselves known.
Despite Wilson’s eloquent writing, “The Piano Lesson,” at nearly three hours, drags on.
The actors are all fine individually, but their magic fails to coalesce.
Wilson’s seminal work is tonally misread, flattened into a sitcom about a haunted piano versus a family struggling to forge anew amid their past.
Richardson Jackson clearly knows how to direct actors and pulls magic out of her cast, creating a production worthy of August Wilson's legacy.
An exquisite revival of August Wilson's The Piano Lesson is pure dramatic pleasure—a richly involving play, beautifully staged, costumed, played, and directed.
She (and Wilson) hand each actor a worthy moment in the spotlight, with every last member of this cast taking full, terrific advantage.

Unfortunately, the production falters in its more explosive moments, with Washington, apparently making his stage acting debut, maintaining such a high energy and decibel level throughout that his unmodulated performance becomes monotonous.
Samuel L. Jackson commands the stage with a performance that is both thunderous and tender, while Danielle Brooks brings remarkable depth to her role as Berniece.

This is a straightforward, well-acted, richly-designed, enjoyable revival that accentuates the competing passions exhibited by Washington and Brooks and the sincere, warmhearted personalities surrounding both of them, including Jackson, Ray Fisher, Trai Byers, and Michael Potts.
It is a scrumptious drama by any measure, and this excellent cast does it honor.
At its best, this production reminds us how Wilson made speech itself swing, and pierce, and inspire.
It’s not in the craftsmanship, but in the assembly, that the piece fails to live up to the finely carved materials that, like its namesake instrument, can truly make this work sing.

Despite the very good performances, there's no real tension, and the only real display of essential chemistry between them comes in a late-second act will they/won't they scene between Brooks and Fisher (as adorable as any potential romance).
If Richardson Jackson saw the dearth of female characters as a problem, her direction turns it into a major flaw.
This is the third production of The Piano Lesson that I've seen and, more than any other, I think it gets to the heart of Wilson's vision.
Ultimately, that splash never comes.
The play ends with a satisfactory conclusion, yet it lacks dramatic closure.
All in all this production didn’t add up for me.
That question looms large in August Wilson's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama.

Long, revealing monologues, the backbone of this particular play, are delivered directly to the audience rather than to the other characters, making them more speeches than important character revelations.
